paras: The attempted lynching of Joe Smith took place at Weedsport, New York, on November 18, 1881, when a mob tried to take Smith, a prisoner accused of outraging and nearly murdering a young woman, from the constable who had brought him there. The constable held the mob off, and the sheriff and a posse kept guard over the prisoner, who "narrowly escaped lynching by the villagers." The episode ran as a short wire item in papers from Maine to Georgia and Tennessee; none of them stated Smith's race.

On November 15 the Dallas Daily Herald reported "a sickening outrage" committed some three days earlier in Wayne County, New York, on a fifteen-year-old sister of Mrs. Charles Hogan of South Butler. That item named the accused as "one Joseph Smith, a laborer," said the girl was "barely alive," and said he was thought to have fled to Oswego and shipped on a vessel to Canada. Later dispatches named the woman as Miss Colwell of Weedsport, placed the crime at South Butler, and said she had been found in the woods nearly dead after a night of exposure, her condition still critical.

According to a dispatch from Auburn dated November 18, Smith was captured in Broome County on Thursday, November 17, and taken to Weedsport the next day. There, "the constable had hard work to prevent the mob from lynching him." The villagers were described as "in a ferment," many believed they would lynch the prisoner before morning, and the sheriff and a posse stood guard.

A second short item from Auburn reported that Smith had "narrowly escaped lynching by the villagers" and that the sheriff and his posse still protected him. A Tennessee weekly placed the escape "At Auburn" on Friday, apparently from the dispatch dateline; the fuller dispatch put the mob at Weedsport.

No report of Smith's trial, of the victim's recovery or death, or of any action against the mob appears in the coverage. The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer added that "if his suffering victim dies he will be lynched," but no later report on the case was found.

Coverage came entirely from the white press and rested on a single Auburn wire, printed on November 19 by the Daily Kennebec Journal, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the Chicago Daily Tribune, the Alexandria Gazette and the National Republican. Shorter versions followed in the Savannah Morning News on November 22, the Spirit of the Age in Vermont on November 23 and the Bolivar Bulletin in Tennessee on December 1.

Headlines such as "Ruffian Captured" in the Kennebec Journal and "Threatened Lynching" in the Alexandria Gazette presented the accusation as fact, and the Chicago Tribune used "Narrowly escaped Being Lynched." Only the Spirit of the Age qualified the charge with "it is charged," while the Dallas Daily Herald, reporting the crime before the capture, called the accused "the fiend." The Lancaster paper ran the item directly after notices of two hangings of "colored men" in Georgia and Arkansas, but it did not describe Smith's race, and no other paper did either.

The reports differ on the victim: the Auburn dispatch named her as Miss Colwell of Weedsport, while the earlier Dallas item described a fifteen-year-old sister of Mrs. Charles Hogan of South Butler. Both versions name Smith and place the crime at South Butler in Wayne County, but no report states that they refer to the same person.

bases: A mob sought to lynch Joe Smith, a prisoner accused of rape and attempted murder, and was held off by a constable, the sheriff and a posse (A2, A4, A6).

Smith was not killed: the constable prevented the mob from lynching him and the sheriff and posse kept guard (A2, A4); the mob acted on the accusation of outrage, but its size is not given, and this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one (A6, A9).
All reports derive from one Auburn, N.Y., wire of Nov. 18 and a short follow-up from the same dateline (A2, A4, A6); the earlier Dallas item describes the crime, not the mob (A1).
